findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review

findings.detail: The paper says the council investment enabled a full regeneration rather than a reduced refurbishment, including public realm, accessibility and an events space. The paper says the events space was first used on 11 July 2026.
findings.matters: A scheme delivered with a stated ratio of council to external funding is an example that finance directors at other councils may want to compare.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant budget rises by £4.3m, assuming the 2027-2028 allocation matches 2026-2027 because it is unconfirmed.
findings.detail: The increase is fully funded by the annual DFG grant allocation from MHCLG. The paper says an update will follow at the next capital monitoring review once allocations are confirmed.
findings.matters: Budgeting on an unconfirmed grant allocation is a risk that finance directors and auditors would check when the allocation is confirmed.

findings.quote: As allocations for 2027-2028 have not been confirmed at the time of writing this report, this is an assumption

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Transformational projects capitalisation rises by £2.6m to fund up-front costs of projects that the paper says will deliver ongoing revenue savings.
findings.detail: The paper says the increase uses additional capital receipts flexibility for identified transformational projects. Such projects would access capital funding, if required, for the up-front costs of delivering revenue savings.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts flexibility to fund transformation costs that aim at revenue savings is an approach that finance directors and auditors would scrutinise.
findings.figures: £2.6m increase in Transformational Projects capitalisation
findings.quote: A £2.6 million increase relating to the Transformational Projects capitalisation

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: Capital receipts assumed in the General Fund total £33.9m, £545k above the approved budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the receipts forecast reflects re-profiled receipts and capital requirements. It also says that only disposals likely to complete are included, and that the forecast will be monitored through the year.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a funding source that depends on asset sales, and a finance director would compare how much of the programme relies on them.
findings.figures: £33.9m capital receipts assumed over 2026-2027 to 2030-2031; £545k increase against the approved budget
findings.quote: This is an increase in a region of £545,000 when compared to the approved budget

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review
findings.headline: External grants and contributions finance 62.3% of the General Fund capital programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the share of external funding is high, most significantly from central government grants and West Midlands Combined Authority funding. It also says the profile of the programme reflects single-year funding settlements and bid-reliant funding.
findings.matters: A high external-funding share ties the programme to grant decisions that are outside the council's control, which is a risk peers and lenders would weigh.
findings.figures: 62.3% of General Fund budget financing from external resources
findings.quote: represent 62.3% of budget financing

findings.headline: External resources assumed for the General Fund programme are reduced by £4.1m.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction is because resources are no longer required, or because assumed external funding has been confirmed at lower levels than anticipated. The paper says this has had no impact on project delivery.
findings.matters: Reductions in assumed external funding are a signal of grant and contribution risk that finance directors track across capital programmes.
findings.figures: £4.1m reduction in external resources

findings.headline: Cost increases in labour, energy and construction materials have led some capital projects to attract higher costs.
findings.detail: The paper says market conditions are beginning to stabilise, but cost pressures remain. It notes that project contingencies are being viewed against these pressures, though significant uncertainty remains.
findings.matters: Construction-cost inflation affecting project budgets is a common pressure, and the paper's stated contingency approach is something peers can compare.
findings.figures: No cost figures given in the paper

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme 2026-2027 to 2030-2031 Quarter Two Review

findings.detail: The paper says the uplift is to ensure sufficient contingency for future budget requirements. Allocations will be made to individual projects using delegations and reported at each quarterly review.
findings.matters: A large uncommitted provision shows how much of the programme is still unallocated, which is relevant when comparing contingency practice across councils.

findings.headline: The A454 Phases 1&2 post-survey works contract, valued at £945,943 over 18 months, is conditional on securing a £1.9 million CRSTS tranche from the West Midlands Combined Authority.

findings.matters: A road scheme's early contract depending on a grant drawdown not yet confirmed, with abortive-spend risk stated, is a funding exposure councils with CRSTS schemes will compare.

findings.paper_title: Procurement - Award of Contracts for Works, Goods and Services
findings.headline: The Bert Williams Leisure Centre decarbonisation contract totals £2.8 million, with £1.5 million funded through the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme and the rest from the Council's capital programme.

findings.headline: Our Future Council 2.0 places all General Fund, HRA and capital budgets within its scope.

findings.matters: Bringing the capital programme and HRA into the same scope as the General Fund sets the policy frame that will govern future borrowing decisions.
findings.quote: All Council budgets will be within scope of Our Future Council, including the General Fund, the Housing Revenue Account and the Capital Programme.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management Activity Monitoring - Mid Year Review 2026-2027

findings.detail: At quarter one these two indicators were forecast to be over their limits. The paper attributes the change to rephasing, not to a reduction in investment.
findings.matters: A council whose prudential indicators moved outside limits and then back within them is reporting a change that peers and lenders monitor for control over borrowing limits.
findings.quote: due to rephasing of service investment activity between financial years they are now within those limits.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management Activity Monitoring - Mid Year Review 2026-2027
findings.headline: CIPFA's revised Treasury Management and Prudential Codes had not been issued at the date of the report, though the paper says results were expected in September.
findings.detail: CIPFA issued its second-round consultation on 1 July 2026, with a closing date of 12 August 2026. The proposed implementation was for the 2027-2028 financial year. The paper says any implications will be reported once the updated Codes are issued.
findings.matters: Every council's treasury and prudential reporting depends on the revised Codes, so a delay affects planning for 2027-2028 across the sector.
findings.quote: However, at the date of writing this report, the revised Codes have not been issued or updates provided.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management Activity Monitoring - Mid Year Review 2026-2027

findings.detail: The capital programme report is subject to the Bilston Health and Wellbeing Facility scheme update and Community Diagnostic Centre proposal being separately approved. The treasury management forecasts and indicators depend on that approval.
findings.matters: A capital scheme that needs separate approval can change the borrowing requirement, which in turn changes the treasury forecast that lenders and peers are using.
findings.quote: Therefore, if this approval is not obtained, the treasury management forecasts and indicators will be amended to reflect this.

findings.headline: Three LOBO loans totaling £17m were called in 2025-2026; the council repaid them at par rather than accept new rates of 6.19-6.26%

Two £5m Dexia LOBOs were called on 26 and 30 January 2026 with proposed rates of 6.21% and 6.26% versus existing rates of 4.26% and 4.29%. The high rates offered (60-173 basis points above existing rates) show market stress on LOBO lending at the time. A lender cares whether the council can refinance when forced to do so; the fact that the council had the liquidity to repay £17m at par demonstrates this capacity, but it also shows the council is exposed to repricing risk when the lender chooses to exercise options.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 School Balances
findings.headline: 33 of 47 schools identified as holding surplus balances above policy thresholds, required to justify their use
findings.detail: The council has set policy thresholds for school balances: 8% of budget for primary, special schools and PRUs; 5% for secondary schools. Schools exceeding these thresholds for two consecutive years or where the authority considers balances a concern are flagged for review. Table 2 shows 33 of 47 schools exceed these thresholds. Section 1.4 states these schools are requested in July to provide plans for use of excess balances by mid-September.
findings.matters: Large reserves held in schools flagged as 'excess' may indicate either prudent financial management or funds not allocated to school purposes; council management of this issue will determine whether reserves are deployed effectively or represent stranded cash
findings.figures: 33 of 47 schools (70%); breakdown: Primary 21 of 29, Secondary 2 of 2, Nursery 6 of 7, Special 1 of 2, Junior 1 of 2, Infant 1 of 2, PRUs 1 of 3
findings.quote: In July all schools that have balances above these criteria are requested to provide plans for the intended use of the excess by mid September.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 School Balances
findings.headline: Schools drawing down balances and entering deficit due to inflation costs and pay awards exceeding budget provision
findings.detail: Section 1.4 notes that schools forecast to use surplus balances are doing so primarily to offset inflation costs and teachers' pay awards exceeding budget percentages forecast in prior years. The same cost drivers are cited in section 1.6 as affecting schools now moving into deficit. This indicates a structural shortfall where schools budgeted for pay increases of X% but faced awards of Y% (where Y exceeds X), combined with inflation not fully provided in original budgets.
findings.matters: If inflation and pay awards are outstripping school budgets, they are likely outstripping council budgets more broadly, signalling cost pressure across the wider authority and a source of future budget pressure
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: We recognise this year schools are likely to see increasing costs associated with inflation and this, alongside the impact of any pay award in excess of budgets, will mean schools with surplus balances are likely to require using these excesses to support the Teachers' Pay Award.

findings.headline: Four schools forecast in deficit for 2023-2024, with Braybrook Centre showing largest deficit of £214k
findings.detail: Table 3 identifies four schools with anticipated deficits in 2023-2024: Castlecroft Primary (£97k), Braybrook Centre (£214k), Penn Fields Special School (£138k), and Phoenix Nursery (£167k). Phoenix Nursery already has an approved licensed deficit. findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 School Balances
findings.headline: School balances forecast to decline from £15.2m to £7.5m in 2023-2024 as all sectors consume reserves
findings.detail: Across all school sectors, Wolverhampton schools are forecast to use £7.8m of reserves in a single financial year. Balances at 31 March 2023 totalled £15.2m across 47 schools; by 31 March 2024 they are forecast to fall to £7.5m. The largest consumer is primary schools (using £3.5m) followed by special schools (£1.3m). At this depletion rate, average school reserves will halve within two years.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion of school financial reserves reduces their ability to absorb cost pressures or unexpected expenditure without council support, and signals underlying structural pressures on school budgets
findings.figures: Balances: £15,236k (31 March 2023) declining to £7,471k (forecast 31 March 2024); Total usage £7,765k; Primary sector: £8,255k to £4,784k (usage £3,471k); Special schools: £1,355k to £89k (usage £1,266k)
findings.quote: The forecast year end financial position as at 31 March 2024 is taken from the submitted budget plans and used to calculate any usage or increase in the school balance carried forward from 31 March 2023 and to forecast the surplus / (deficit) balance for 31 March 2024.

findings.headline: Council adds guiding principle on retaining and attracting talent for transformation delivery

findings.matters: Adding a workforce retention principle signals anticipated significant organizational change ahead; emphasis on securing key staff suggests concern about stability during a challenging transformation period.

findings.quote: we must continue to retain and attract the best talent and capacity so that we can deliver the priorities, for our City, efficiency and effectivity

findings.paper_title: Appendix3 Our Approach and Guiding Principles
findings.headline: Council will shift from universal service levels to targeted, data-driven approaches where affordable on an across-the-board basis
findings.detail: Recognizing that universal service levels cannot be afforded in all cases, the council will move to targeted approaches based on data and evidence, supported by digital technology. This applies even to services for vulnerable adults and children.
findings.matters: Service rationing and targeting directly affect fiscal sustainability and service coverage; this signals material operational changes with implications for financial planning and service user outcomes.
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: Universal services (i.e. standard / across the board service levels) are unlikely to be affordable in all instances, it will therefore be necessary to move towards a more targeted approach in some areas, this will be based on data and evidence and will utilise digital technology

findings.paper_title: Appendix3 Our Approach and Guiding Principles
findings.headline: Council plans to rationalize and consolidate assets to generate capital receipts for transformation funding
findings.detail: Asset rationalization is explicitly designed both to reduce ongoing costs and generate capital receipts that will fund the Our Future Council programme. Sites released will be directed to housing and regeneration to create additional economic benefit.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a critical funding source for local government transformation; understanding the asset plan and expected receipt scale matters for assessing financial sustainability and programme delivery risk.
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: significantly rationalise and reorganise our assets and consolidate them in communities – as well as reducing costs and generating capital receipts, that will support the delivery of Our Future Council, sites will be released for housing and other regeneration, which will also create jobs and training opportunities

findings.paper_title: Appendix3 Our Approach and Guiding Principles
findings.headline: Council will restrict new borrowing to only essential services with financial or economic returns or that lever external funding
findings.detail: Guiding principle explicitly limits borrowing to cases where capital expenditure is essential to day-to-day services and either delivers a financial or economic return on investment, or leverages significant external capital funding. This represents a formal discipline on new borrowing decisions.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing covenant strength and credit risk need to understand a council's borrowing discipline; an explicit restriction to essential, return-generating investment signals tighter fiscal control and lower debt expansion risk.
findings.figures: none provided
findings.quote: will continue to be prudent with all borrowing and will only borrow where it is essential to do so and where the capital expenditure is required to support essential day to day services, and / or delivers a return on the investment (whether that be a financial and/or economic return) and / or it levers in significant external capital funding to support essential day to day services

However, early indications show emerging cost pressures, particularly in adult social care and resident services. Services identifying pressures are required to put in place recovery plans to mitigate them.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess financial sustainability partly by whether councils need to raid reserves to balance budgets; emerging cost pressures in social care are material given demographic demand and cost inflation.
findings.figures: £396.2 million net budget requirement; £8.4 million approved savings targets
findings.quote: The Council was again able to set a balanced budget for 2026-2027 without the need to use general fund reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Financial management risk score steady at 8/8; council depends on limited reserves to cushion expenditure overruns
findings.detail: The Financial Management risk notes that weak financial controls could cause expenditure to exceed budget, forcing a call on reserves. The council flags that its reserve position is limited. The risk score has not improved despite being on the register for years, suggesting this is a structural rather than cyclical concern.
findings.matters: Limited reserves and budget-overspend risk go together. A finance director needs to know how much reserve buffer the council has and whether it is being eroded by uncontrollable pressures.
findings.figures: Risk score 8/8 (current and target, unchanged); described as 'limited reserves'
findings.quote: If the Council does not have strong financial management there is a risk that the expenditure will exceed the budget, leading to a call on the limited reserves that are available to support the financial sustainability and transformation of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: CQC inspection outcome no longer poses risk of Inadequate rating; inspection completed June 2025, outcome awaited
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) conducted an onsite inspection of Adult Social Care in June 2025 and fed back positive informal comments with no serious concerns noted. The council received an updated (but not yet finalised) report in May 2026. As of the register update, the council is confident that an Inadequate rating is now very unlikely, and has downgraded the risk accordingly. Final outcome expected by 22 May 2026.
findings.matters: An Inadequate CQC rating would trigger enforcement and reputational damage. De-escalation of this risk is good news for financial and reputational resilience.
findings.figures: Risk score 6/6 (current and target, unchanged); onsite inspection June 2025; informal feedback no serious concerns
findings.quote: May 2026 – Updated report received but not yet finalised. Meeting held with CQC April 2026 with outcome expected by 22 May 2026. Inadequate rating now very unlikely, therefore risk scoring updated.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Agresso core financial system SaaS migration carries risk of implementation failure; system underpins all financial reporting and controls
findings.detail: The council's migration to Agresso as a Software-as-a-Service platform is at risk of slipping or implementation failure. The register notes this could significantly impact the council's core financial systems. Agresso holds all transactional financial data and sits at the heart of budget management, reporting, and audit controls. Risk score is 12/12.
findings.matters: A failed core financial system migration creates audit, compliance, and reporting risks. A finance director or auditor needs to know whether this is on track and whether there is a fallback plan.
findings.figures: Risk score 12/12 (current and target); no recent update on implementation progress visible
findings.quote: There is a risk the Council's Agresso SaaS migration is not successfully implemented in time resulting in the Council's core financial systems being significantly impacted and posing a reputational risk to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Energy from Waste plant holds highest risk score (20); no mitigation progress noted since March 2026
findings.detail: The council's Energy from Waste plant remains at maximum risk score (20/20). The risk is of non-operation due to major fire, breakdown, or unavailability of skilled contractors. This is a critical service and asset—failure would force waste diversion to alternative (expensive) disposal methods. Risk direction is unchanged (no improvement) and no update on mitigation progress is recorded in the June 2026 register.
findings.matters: A critical infrastructure asset at maximum risk with no visible improvement plan signals operational resilience exposure and potential cost shocks.
findings.figures: Risk score 20/20 (current and previous), target 9; risk rating unchanged since March 2026
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Energy from Waste (EfW) plant may become unavailable or non-operational, for example, due to significant fire or breakdown or the unavailability of a suitably skilled contractor to operate and maintain the plant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Safeguarding Adults caseload increasing month-on-month; recruitment challenges in social work limiting response capacity
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care directorate is experiencing sustained month-on-month growth in safeguarding referrals. A restructure has now concluded but the transition phase is creating capacity pressures, compounded by difficulties recruiting suitably skilled social workers—agency staff are being used to fill gaps but supply is constrained. 45% of referrals are being assessed as inappropriate, but triaging them remains a workload.
findings.matters: A growing safeguarding caseload that cannot be staffed at pace creates a service delivery risk and a call on non-social-care budgets. It signals labour-market constraints beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Month-on-month increase in referrals; 45% of referrals currently assessed as inappropriate; social workers and agency staff filling gaps; target risk score 6 (current and target)
findings.quote: There continues to be a month on month increase in Safeguarding referrals which impacts on the ability of Adult Social Care to ensure a timely response and has led to an increase in the time enquiries are taking. Whilst we have responded to the risks with additional temporary posts there are challenges with recruitment and shortage of suitably skilled agency social workers to fill temporary vacancies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Private sector damp and mould complaints increased in winter 2024–25; service warns it cannot scale response without additional funding
findings.detail: Private rented housing damp and mould complaints have increased significantly again in the latest winter season after a high-demand winter 2023–24. The council's Private Sector Housing Service is responding reactively. The team explicitly warns that without additional resource and funding, serious mould cases cannot be treated as 'business as usual' and reactive management will continue. Cost-of-living pressures are deepening the problem.
findings.matters: Growing tenant health complaints in a sector the council has no direct control over but statutory duty for signals cost and resource risk. The explicit warning of inadequate funding is a flag.
findings.figures: Risk score 8/8 (current and target); serious complaint numbers increased winter 2024–25
findings.quote: Without additional resource and funding, dealing with serious mould cases cannot be established as a 'business as usual' work stream and the service will continue to respond reactively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator issued C2 grading on 28 January 2026 citing weaknesses in consumer standards delivery; improvement required
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing graded the council C2 (Compliance with Concerns) with no serious failings noted, but in line with the council's own self-referral flagging weaknesses in delivering consumer standards outcomes. The council is now required to develop and deliver an Improvement Strategy with a Regulatory Compliance Board oversighting progress. The timing and pace of improvement delivery are under review.
findings.matters: A regulator-issued C rating creates enforcement risk and reputational exposure. It signals operational and governance weaknesses in a major asset base (council housing) and creates compliance costs.
findings.figures: C2 grading issued 28 January 2026; Impact score 4 (critical), likelihood score 4 (likely)
findings.quote: On 28 January 2026 the Regulator of Social Housing issued CWC a C2 grading, noting no serious failings, and in line with our self-referral that 'weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards'

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Housing waiting list now exceeds 8,200 residents; council securing £19 million Homes England grant but supply-demand gap remains
findings.detail: Demand for council accommodation is increasing significantly with over 8,200 residents on the waiting list. The council faces pressure to place homeless households in temporary accommodation, a cost driver. However, the council has secured grant funding (first in the country for Homes England Portfolio Partner initiative providing up to £19 million) and is progressing multiple regeneration and new-build schemes. A 23% net increase in homes is targeted through estate masterplans.
findings.matters: A growing housing waiting list creates uncontrollable budget pressure through temporary accommodation spend. A lender needs to see whether the council has a credible plan to close the supply-demand gap and how long that will take.
findings.figures: Over 8,200 registered for council accommodation; £19 million Homes England Portfolio Partner grant; 23% net increase targeted through estate regeneration
findings.quote: the waiting list is increasing significantly (over 8200 registered for council accommodation), and vulnerable residents may need rehousing in temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Repairs budget overspend being driven by surge in damp and mould referrals; housing service faces resource constraints
findings.detail: Council-owned housing is experiencing a significant increase in damp and mould complaints, particularly in winter months. The council has had to reallocate staffing and financial resources to respond, but contractor capacity is constrained by regional labour shortages. The repairs budget is overspending as a result. The council notes 2% of inspections identify Category 1 hazards under HHSRS but cannot scale response without additional resources.

findings.quote: Staffing and financial resources have needed to be reallocated to DMC to meet the increase in demand. Contractors have also been requested to increase labour resources. This has had limited success due to the region wide shortage in suitable labour. The repairs budget overspend is contributed to by DMC requests.

A lender watches whether councils stay within their own self-determined limits, as drift signals loss of control.

findings.headline: Three LOBO loans were called and rejected as lenders offered penalty rates; council managing debt in stressed market.
findings.detail: During 2025-2026, three Lender Option Borrower Option loans totalling £17 million were called. Lenders offered new rates ranging from 6.19% to 6.26%, significantly above the loans' current rates (3.60% to 4.29%). Wolverhampton rejected all proposals and repaid the loans instead. This shows the council is watchful for lender opportunism but also signals the debt refinancing market is becoming challenging.
findings.matters: LOBO calls with punitive rates are a stress signal in the public debt market. A lender to the council needs to understand that refinancing older borrowing is becoming more expensive and that the council is actively managing to avoid being trapped into higher rates. This affects future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £17.0 million total LOBO principal called; proposed rates 6.19%, 6.21%, 6.26% versus current rates of 3.60%, 4.26%, 4.29%
findings.quote: Due to current market conditions some LOBO lenders are 'calling' their options and offering inflated long term rates deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted. In order to be prudent, the potential for these 'calls' are included in the Council's cashflow projections to ensure that if called, the Council are in a position to repay the loans to avoid these higher rates.

findings.figures: Medium-term capital programme £352.6 million (2024-25 to 2029-30); 2025-2026 outturn £70.2 million against revised budget £87.1 million
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty and cost pressures which continue to affect the capital investment programme. Rising construction costs, particularly in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions are impacting on project budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Children's social care cost growth is explicitly flagged as a particular challenge
findings.detail: Among medium-term pressures facing the council (including pay inflation and general demand growth), increases in children's social care costs are specifically identified as a particular challenge. The council also faces increased demand pressures in adult social care.
findings.matters: Children's social care is demand-driven, difficult to control, and a known area of overspend across councils. Its specific callout here suggests the council views it as a material risk that may continue to drive budget pressures despite savings plans.
findings.figures: 2026-2027 budget £396.2 million; savings targets £8.4 million
findings.quote: Like many other local authorities, the Council continues to be faced with pressures over the medium term, such as pay and other inflationary related pressures, increases in costs within children's social care being a particular challenge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Medium-term deficit projections improved significantly after funding settlement, but deficits remain forecast for 2027-2028 and 2028-2029
findings.detail: In February 2025, the council projected a £23.5 million deficit for 2027-2028. Following the February 2026 funding settlement (Fair Funding Review), this projection improved to £3.8 million for the same year, though it then rises to £14.8 million by 2028-2029. This material improvement in outlook reflects changes to central government funding allocation favouring higher-deprivation councils.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' medium-term sustainability through multi-year projections. The improvement is positive but the remaining deficits show continued financial challenges that must be managed through delivery of the council's Our Future Council savings programme.
findings.figures: 2027-2028 deficit: £23.5 million (Feb 2025 projection) reduced to £3.8 million (Feb 2026 projection); 2028-2029 projected deficit £14.8 million
findings.quote: In February 2026, it was reported that the updated projected budget deficit was £3.8 million for 2027-2028 (compared to £23.5 million previously), rising to £14.8 million by 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Final Audit and Risk Committee Report - Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026
findings.headline: All 17 Financial Management Code standards now assessed as green after improvement of one previously amber standard

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Reserves
findings.headline: Future Years Budget Strategy Reserve held with £2m already committed for forward spending
findings.detail: The council holds £7.6m in this reserve specifically to 'support the budget strategy in future years,' with £2m already approved for commitment. This indicates the council expects budget pressures ahead and is building a specific buffer to manage them.
findings.matters: Deliberate provisioning for future budget gaps suggests the council anticipates structural pressures; reliance on reserves rather than in-year solutions may limit flexibility.

findings.quote: Funds available to support the budget strategy in future years.

findings.detail: Schools balances fell from £13.4m to £11.7m with a transfer out of £4.4m. This represents significant drawdown from what may be a key buffer against rising school spending pressures, particularly given national cost pressures in education.

These reserves fund the 'Our Future Council Transformation Strategy' to 'deliver greater efficiencies.' findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Homelessness placements fell to 64 families in Q4 from 121 in Q3; average time in temporary accommodation 149 days
findings.detail: The number of families successfully moved into secure housing fell sharply from 121 in Q3 to 64 in Q4 2025-2026. The council attributes this to constraints in property availability and shortage of suitable move-on options, not reduced demand. Time spent in temporary accommodation remains high at 149 days average, indicating households are spending extended periods in temporary housing.
findings.matters: A sharp quarterly collapse in homelessness placements indicates a structural shortage of available housing and move-on options that the council cannot resolve. This represents an unfunded statutory duty and potential pressure on housing and temporary accommodation budgets, with possible implications for other council services.
findings.figures: 121 families placed in Q3; 64 families placed in Q4 (47% drop); 149 days average time in temporary accommodation
findings.quote: Homelessness outcomes are showing signs of deterioration, with the number of families moved into secure housing falling from 121 in Q3 to 64 by the end of Q4, despite higher levels earlier in the year (peaking at 140 in Q2 2025-2026). This decline reflects ongoing constraints in property availability, rather than reduced demand, alongside a shortage of suitable move‑on options within the system.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Parking income shortfall creating £732,000 overspend, indicating possible weakness in city centre footfall or changed travel patterns.
findings.detail: Parking services is reporting a £732,000 overspend comprised of income shortfall, additional operating costs, and pressures within parking enforcement. The combination of lower income alongside cost growth is a negative indicator for a service expected to contribute positively to general fund.
findings.matters: Parking income shortfalls often signal reduced city centre vitality, lower commuter footfall, or changed transport patterns. This trend, combined with rising operating costs, suggests structural economic weakness affecting a key council income source.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG accumulated deficit of £16.4 million, partially dependent on government grant of up to 90% whose level and conditions remain undefined.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block component of Dedicated Schools Grant has accumulated a deficit of £16.4 million by end of March 2026, with an in-year deficit of £10.4 million. The council uses a statutory accounting override to carry this outside the main revenue budget. Government announced in February 2026 a High Needs Stability Grant to assist authorities, with payment due summer 2026 covering up to 90% of the deficit. However, the grant amount depends on government assessment of eligible expenditure and local authorities meeting undefined conditions, creating uncertainty.
findings.matters: A £16.4 million accumulated deficit represents a contingent liability. While government may cover up to 90%, reliance on government discretion on eligible costs and undefined conditions creates budget uncertainty. If grant is lower than maximum or conditions unmet, the council could face a significant unexpected cost.
findings.figures: £16.4 million accumulated High Needs Block deficit at 31 March 2026; £10.4 million in-year deficit; maximum government grant up to 90% of £14.1 million net position
findings.quote: The High Needs Block of Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) ended 2025-2026 with an in-year deficit of £10.4 million. The total accumulated deficit against the High Needs Block grant is £16.4 million at the end of 2025-2026. Currently for accounting purposes there is a statutory override which means we can carry forward a deficit balance outside of the Council's main revenue budget. In February 2026 Government announced its intention to pay a High Needs Stability Grant to assist local authorities with DSG deficits. The grant is due to be paid in the summer of 2026 which will be up to a maximum value of 90% of the £14.1 million accrued net deficit as at 31 March 2026, recognised in the unusable reserve. The level of grant is currently unknown and will depend on what Government deems to be eligible expenditure and local authorities meeting other conditions.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £3.4 million in complex placements despite £7.6 million additional budget, with £5.0 million more required for 2026-2027.
findings.detail: The Children and Young People In Care service overspent by £3.4 million in 2025-2026 driven by costs of complex residential and care packages. This occurred despite £7.6 million additional budget being allocated during the year. The council is committing a further £5.0 million for 2026-2027 plus £1.0 million corporate contingency to manage projected demand and cost inflation.
findings.matters: Cost growth in a provider-led market for complex placements is volatile and hard to control. Repeated budget increases failing to prevent overspends suggests the council has limited control over cost growth and faces material risk of further deficits if placements or complexity increase further.
findings.figures: £3.4 million overspend in 2025-2026; £7.6 million additional budget provided in year; £5.0 million additional budget plus £1.0 million contingency committed for 2026-2027
findings.quote: The main pressures are seen in the Children and Young People In Care service totalling £3.4 million due to increased cost of complex residential and care packages including Children with Disabilities and Short Breaks in a provider led market. This is after additional budget of £7.6 million in Children and Young People In Care service to support cost pressures. The 2026-2027 budget incorporates £5.0 million of additional budget to support increases due to demand and cost inflation for care packages with additional budget contingency totalling £1.0 million held corporately.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £2.8 million despite £11 million additional budget, with a further £12.5 million committed for 2026-2027.
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care directorate overspent by £2.8 million in 2025-2026 even after receiving £11.0 million additional budget during the year. The overspend is driven by increased demand for care packages and rising complexity of need. The council has pre-committed a further £12.5 million for 2026-2027, indicating the council expects cost pressures to continue escalating.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends despite rising budget allocations signal a structural cost problem that cannot be solved by incremental budget increases alone. A lender would worry about the council's ability to absorb further cost growth or whether reserves are being used to offset ongoing deficits.
findings.figures: £2.8 million overspend (2.41% of £116.2 million budget); £11.0 million additional budget provided in 2025-2026; £12.5 million additional budget allocated for 2026-2027
findings.quote: The Adult Social Care directorate is reporting an outturn overspend of £2.8 million (2.41%) against a net controllable budget of £116.2 million. The overspend mainly relates to increased demand for care packages across Safeguarding and Ageing Well Service and Disabilities and Mental Health Service. This overspend is after additional budget of £11.0 million being incorporated into the 2025-2026 budget. The 2026-2027 Budget incorporates additional budget totalling £12.5 million to support both projected increases in demand and fee uplifts for 2026-2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Savings targets profiling was 'ambitious' in February 2025 budget and is now being extended
findings.detail: The council approved £31.8 million in recurrent savings for 2025-2026 to 2027-2028. In the current budget, it acknowledges that 'the profiling and level of some savings targets was ambitious' and is now reprofiling some savings 'over a longer period of time in order that they can be delivered in a more considered way'. It is also removing approximately £1.2 million of originally planned savings. A £2.8 million contingency for slippage/non-delivery exists in 2026-2027, with a further £1.0 million added in November 2025 (though this November addition has now been removed).
findings.matters: Admitting that approved savings were over-ambitious and requiring reprofiling suggests execution risk; councils often miss savings targets
findings.figures: £31.8m recurrent savings approved, ~£1.2m removed, £2.8m contingency for slippage
findings.quote: It was recognised that in February 2025, the profiling and level of some savings targets was ambitious. In light of the favourable funding settlement a number of changes are now proposed. This includes reprofiling some approved savings over a longer period of time in order that they can be delivered in a more considered way and thereby lessening the impact on service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Children's social care requiring additional £2.0 million on top of £4.0 million approved just 12 months earlier
findings.detail: The council approved £4.0 million additional budget in February 2025 for children's social care pressures (complexity of placements in a provider-led market). It now requires a further £2.0 million in 2026-2027, with £1.0 million held corporately and released in-year. Future years have been re-assumed upward. The pattern of repeated upward revisions within 12 months suggests underlying costs are outpacing initial estimates.
findings.matters: Repeated upward revisions to a single service budget after such short notice suggests cost control is inadequate or demand has fundamentally changed
findings.figures: £4.0m approved Feb 2025, additional £2.0m required (£1.0m held corporately)
findings.quote: Based on the latest financial modelling it is now proposed to increase this budget by a further £2.0 million in 2026-2027, of which £1.0 million will be held corporately and released during the year if required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Government Social Care Fair Pay Policy (2028-2029 rollout) costs unquantified but included in MTFS
findings.detail: Government is consulting on a Social Care Fair Pay Policy including a national pay agreement, legally enforceable conditions, and annual collective bargaining, rolling out 2028-2029. The council has 'made some high level assumptions and have incorporated these into the medium-term financial strategy' but explicitly flags these as 'early high level indicative projections and will be subject to change'. Government response expected Spring 2026; the council cannot yet quantify the impact or whether additional funding will cover it.
findings.matters: A new national pay floor for social care could materially increase costs; the council has signalled it cannot quantify this risk, indicating exposure to a material unplanned cost
findings.figures: Roll-out 2028-29; costs unspecified
findings.quote: However, in order to be prudent we have made some high level assumptions and have incorporated these into the medium-term financial strategy. These are however, early high level indicative projections and will be subject to change. Updates will be provided to Councillors in future reports.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Council required to use £2.0 million from reserves and capital receipts to balance 2026-2027 budget
findings.detail: The council must draw £2.0 million of one-off resources (capital receipts or earmarked reserves) to fund transformation and balance the 2026-2027 budget. Separately, £11.4 million in prior-year one-off items are reversing: including £5.0 million in capital receipts, £1.703 million in one-off grants, and £1.2 million in dividends. The council states its 'ultimate aim' is to 'remove the reliance on earmarked reserves to balance the budget', but this has not yet been achieved.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance a recurrent budget is unsustainable; it indicates core revenue cannot fund core spending and the council is consuming its financial buffer
findings.figures: £2.0m required 2026-27, £11.4m reversal of prior one-offs (£5.0m receipts, £1.703m grants, £1.2m dividends)
findings.quote: the Council is required to use £2.0 million of one-off resources (earmarked reserves / capital receipts) in order to fund transformation activity and balance the budget for 2026-2027

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG deficit of £6.0 million reported for the first time in 2024-2025
findings.detail: The council reported a £6.0 million deficit on the High Needs Block (SEND funding) for the first time, with a total DSG deficit of £4.9 million. A statutory override allows this to be held on the balance sheet until March 2028, masking cash impact. Government will cover 90% of historic deficits via a High Needs Stability Grant from 2026-2027 (subject to a SEND reform plan), but the council is assuming a further £2.0 million cost pressure in 2028-2029. This suggests the underlying deficit is unresolved and will recur once the override ends.
findings.matters: A first-time deficit of this scale in education funding signals a structural problem; the statutory override mechanism expires March 2028 and provides false comfort about the sustainability of SEND spending

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Pay award for 2026-2027 unresolved, with every 1% above the 3% assumption creating £2 million annual cost
findings.detail: The council's budget assumes 3% for 2026-2027 and 2.5% thereafter, but the actual award remains unagreed. Any overshoot would require funding from 'corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies and reserves' or would increase the projected deficit. The sensitivity is acute: each percentage point above assumption = £2.0 million per annum, and this sensitivity compounds across the workforce.
findings.matters: Public sector pay typically settles above initial assumptions; this sensitivity suggests the council has minimal budget flexibility to absorb realistic pay outcomes
findings.quote: At the time of writing this report the pay award for 2026-2027 has not been agreed. Our budget proposals, assume that the pay award will be 3% in 2026-2027, and 2.5% in 2027-2028 and 2028-2029... For every 1% increase in pay award costs, there is an additional budget pressure of circa £2.0 million per annum.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Adult social care costs rising to £12.5 million pressure in 2026-2027, up from £10.0 million previously assumed
findings.detail: The council identified £8.0 million in costs from proposed care provider fee uplifts and demographic growth, plus £4.5 million in in-year pressures from 2025-2026. Future projections show £13.0 million (2027-28) and £14.0 million (2028-29). The council notes it is 'confident that with a combination of the additional budget mentioned above, the impact of the 2026-2027 pay award (which is currently held corporately), along with the corporate contingency held to support any in-year pressures within Adult Social Care we will remain above our notional target', but this requires drawing on contingencies.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a council's largest controllable cost; repeated upward revisions within a single budget cycle suggest demand is outpacing funding and cost control is weak
findings.quote: The estimated cost of the proposed fee uplift along with assumptions around demographic growth are projected to cost circa £8.0 million. In addition, we are also seeing in-year (2025-2026) pressures and the projected impact for 2026-2027 is forecast to be a further £4.5 million, giving a total projected cost pressure of £12.5 million for 2026-2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Service and commercial investment debt forecast to peak at 63.9% loan-to-value in 2027-28
findings.detail: Net debt for service/commercial investments (WV Living, Help to Own, investment properties) rises from £30.7m (2025-26) to £41.3m (2027-28), with loan-to-value ratio increasing from 57.3% to peak at 63.9%. Council acknowledges downside risk: if asset fair value falls below borrowing level, Strategic Executive Board would need to reassess whether investments deliver strategic objectives. Investment returns are declining; income falls from 1.5% to 0.9% of net service expenditure.
findings.matters: Rising leverage on commercial assets, combined with council's explicit risk acknowledgment, creates potential for covenant pressure or forced asset sales if valuations decline. Falling investment returns suggest expected returns not materializing.
findings.figures: Net debt £30.7m (2025-26) to £41.3m (2027-28); loan-to-value 57.3% rising to 63.9% (2027-28); investment income 1.5% declining to 0.9% of net service expenditure
findings.quote: In the event that the fair value of the investment is no longer sufficient to provide security against the loss the Strategic Executive Board will need to consider whether the investment is enabling wider strategic objectives.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund capital programme assumes £43.5m in capital receipts from planned asset disposals
findings.detail: Council plans significant asset rationalization to generate capital receipts and reduce costs. £43.5m in capital receipts is assumed across the five-year programme (2025-26 to 2030-31). The council requires detailed review of disposal schedules 'to identify only those that are likely to be completed,' indicating execution risk around meeting the receipts target.
findings.matters: Asset sales are volatile funding source. Large assumed receipts create financing risk if disposals don't materialize; failure to achieve target would require capital programme cuts or increased borrowing.
findings.figures: £43.5 million capital receipts assumed over five years (2025-26 to 2030-31)
findings.quote: Capital receipts totalling £43.5 million have been assumed within the General Fund capital investment programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Council pursuing major restructuring through 'Our Future Council' in response to acknowledged financial challenges
findings.detail: In November 2024, Cabinet approved Our Future Council (OFC), explicitly recognizing significant financial challenges. OFC includes asset rationalization to generate capital receipts, becoming 'funder of last resort,' and prudent borrowing only. Strategic Asset Plan is being refreshed to align with OFC principles, with new plan implementation scheduled for 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether a council facing financial stress has board-level recognition and response strategy. OFC being approved and guiding capital planning indicates material financial challenge requiring structural reform.
findings.figures: November 2024 approval; new asset plan for 2026 implementation
findings.quote: In November 2024, Cabinet approved the approach and guiding principles of Our Future Council (OFC) in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: £2.5m of £25.2m approved savings at risk in 2025-2026; 2026-2027 budget incorporates £8.4m new savings
findings.detail: The paper reports that of £25.2m of approved savings in 2025-2026, £2.5m is at risk of delivery, of which £1.5m is being mitigated by other efficiencies. External audit has noted 'improved arrangements in place to identify and report against savings delivery'. The 2026-2027 budget incorporates only £8.4m of new savings, down from previous larger programmes. Corporate contingency is held against delivery slippage.
findings.matters: Savings of ~10% of the corporate contingency at risk signals execution is real but not guaranteed; the shift to smaller annual savings (£8.4m vs historical £40m+ programmes) may reflect either prudence or delivery constraint.
findings.quote: we reported in November 2025 in the Performance and Budget Monitoring report that out of the £25.2 million of approved savings in 2025-2026, only £2.5 million was at risk of delivery, of which £1.5 million was being mitigated against by other efficiencies

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: External audit delivered clean opinion but flagged financial resilience as ongoing concern
findings.detail: In January 2026, the council received an unqualified audit opinion on accounts and external auditors reported no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance or VFM. However, auditors raised two recommendations specifically under financial sustainability: on Dedicated School Grant and on financial plans over short and medium term to manage financial resilience risk. Both are acknowledged by council and in the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.matters: While the clean audit opinion is reassuring, the auditor's specific concerns about DSG and financial resilience planning suggest these are known vulnerabilities; DSG deficits are a widespread sector issue that can create balance sheet pressure.
findings.figures: Unqualified audit opinion; 2 financial sustainability recommendations raised
findings.quote: External Audit raised only two improvement recommendations under financial sustainability in respect of Dedicated School Grant and financial plans in place over the short and medium term to manage the risk of financial resilience. Both of which are already recognised by the Council and incorporated into the Strategic Risk Register

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Budget still relies on £2m of one-off resources (reserves/capital receipts) despite overall balance claim
findings.detail: Although the paper describes 2026-2027 as 'a balanced budget', it requires £2.0m of one-off resources (earmarked reserves or capital receipts) to balance it. This is an improvement on 2025-2026 (£5m), but the Section 151 Officer explicitly states this 'is not a sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium term estimated financial gap'. One-off resources can only smooth, not solve.
findings.matters: One-off resource use signals underlying budget deficit is not covered by recurring income; even at £2m per year this depletes reserves (current uncommitted earmarked reserves £32.6m) and is unsustainable beyond the near term.
findings.figures: £2.0m one-off resources required in 2026-2027; uncommitted earmarked reserves £32.6m
findings.quote: In the opinion of the Section 151 Officer, the proposed use of earmarked reserves during 2026-2027 is prudent, proportionate and in line with the approved budget strategy for 2026-2027, however, this is not an ongoing sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium financial challenge

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Pay award assumption of 3% carries material unfunded risk: each 1% above costs £2m per annum
findings.detail: The budget assumes a 3% pay award for 2026-2027 (actual award not yet known at report date). The paper states that every 1% increase above 3% costs approximately £2m per annum. With no contingency above this rate flagged in the budget narrative, any higher award would need to be funded from corporate contingency (already carrying other risks) or reserves.
findings.matters: Unfunded pay inflation is an immediate P&L hit that cannot be deferred; public sector pay awards are politically difficult to manage down; a 5% award would create a £4m unplanned deficit.
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumed; £2m cost per 1% increase
findings.quote: For every 1% increase in pay award costs, there is an additional budget pressure of circa £2.0 million per annum. Any increase above the 3% currently built into the budget for 2026-2027 would need to be funded from a combination of corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies and reserves

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Overall budget risk remains RED despite improvements; material uncertainty from 2028-2029 due to government policy changes
findings.detail: Despite the improved deficit position, the Section 151 Officer maintains a RED risk rating for the MTFS, citing medium-term forecasting risks, service demand risks (particularly social care), and potential cost implications from government policy changes (SEND accounting override end, Social Care Fair Pay Policy, UK Emissions Trading Scheme from 2028). The paper explicitly states these policy impacts are uncertain in quantum.
findings.matters: A RED risk rating on a three-year strategy signals that management do not consider the forecasts robust beyond 2026-2027; unknown government policy costs from 2028 create contingent liabilities that don't yet have provisions.
findings.figures: Overall risk rated RED; Government policy changes create uncertainties from 2028-2029

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029

findings.matters: Growing statutory service obligations (social care is undefeasible) create structural budget pressure that cannot be cut without service failure; a lender needs to know if this trajectory can be sustained through the lending term.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Cabinet asked to raise capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton Council's Cabinet is asked on 18 November to raise its capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m, an increase of £2.561m. The report says approval for the increase is sought in that report.

The council's forecast papers, in an appendix setting out detailed changes, give the reason as "additional use of capital receipts flexibility to fund specific transformational projects". Capital receipts are the money a council raises from selling assets.

The appendix does not name the projects in the material reviewed. The £2m is the currently approved budget and £4.561m is the proposed figure.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton's high needs schools spending ended 2025-26 £10.4m over, against £6.8m forecast in budget
news_drafts.lead:
Spending on support for children with special educational needs in Wolverhampton ended 2025-26 at £10.4m over budget, the Schools' Forum heard on 15 October. The council's budget in February 2025 had expected an overspend of £6.8m on the "high needs" part of school funding, which covers children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending was £62.08m against a budget of £51.72m, a 19.9% overrun.

The largest single driver was top-up payments to schools for pupils with special needs. These were £29.62m against a budget of £26.91m, an overspend of £2.72m, or 10%. The paper says the increase was part of the overspend already indicated at the third quarter. Within top-up funding, special schools and alternative provision (education outside mainstream schools) took £1.9m of additional spend, and exceptional needs funding, for specialist equipment and one-to-one support, rose £340,000, or 15%, on the previous year. Independent provision for under-16s within the city ran £0.83m (17%) over, at £5.70m against £4.87m. Provision outside the city came in £0.61m (7%) under.

Other parts of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) partly offset the overspend. The Schools Block had a £0.5m surplus and the Early Years Block a £0.4m underspend. The net deficit held in the council's unusable reserve for the grant stood at £9.2m at year-end, up £4.3m from £4.9m a year earlier.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Pensions Board: auditors expect unmodified opinion on £23,368.6m pension fund accounts
news_drafts.lead:
Auditors of the West Midlands Pension Fund expect to give an unmodified opinion, meaning a sign-off without qualification, on its accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026. The draft accounts, in the audit findings report put to the Pensions Board on 13 October 2026, show net assets of £23,368.6m at that date. The report says the audit identified no adjustments affecting the fund's reported financial position and met no significant difficulties or significant matters.

The auditors did identify £20.7m of unadjusted differences in the valuation of the fund's investments as at 31 March 2026, above the £10.9m reporting threshold. The report attributes the overstatement to the timing of information for pension fund reporting compared with the audit date of the underlying investment funds. Management proposes not to amend the statements, on the basis that the differences "are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively".

Testing of employer contributions also found £14.1m of early retirement costs relating to 2024/25 that were recorded in 2025/26. The fund's accounting policy says such contributions are accounted for in the period in which the liability arises. Management assessed the amount as immaterial and made no prior-year restatement. The auditors recommended that management ensure transactions are recognised in line with the fund's accounting policies.
